RIO DE JANEIRO, Brazil (CNN) -- Former presidents of Mexico, Colombia and Brazil called Wednesday for the decriminalization of marijuana for personal use and a change in tactics on the war on drugs, a Spanish news agency said. People march in support of legalized marijuana in late January in Belem, northern Brazil. Ex-presidents Ernesto Zedillo of Mexico, Cesar Gaviria of Colombia and Fernando Henrique Cardoso of Brazil made their announcement at a meeting in Brazil of the Latin American Commission on Drugs and Democracy, the EFE news agency said. "The problem is that current policies are based on prejudices and fears and not on results," Gaviria said at a news conference in which the commission's recommendations were presented. The 17-member panel worked on the report for a year and will forward it to all Latin American governments as well as the United States and the European Union, EFE said. Gaviria said the time is right to start a debate on the subject, particularly with the pragmatic openings provided by the election of President Barack Obama in the United States. "In many states in the United States, as is the case in California, they have begun to change federal policies with regard to tolerating marijuana for therapeutic purposes. And in Washington there's some consensus that the current policy is failing," EFE quotes Gaviria as saying. Decriminalization should be accompanied by treatment for addicts and public service campaigns on abuse prevention, the commission said. "If you don't help those who are dependent, you are half way there because they are going to commit crime to get money and pay for the drug," Gaviria said. Cardoso said the group called for only the decriminalization of marijuana and not other illicit drugs because "you have to start somewhere" and it would have been unrealistic to ask the same for all drugs, EFE said. Marijuana was chosen because it is grown in all countries in the region and because it is "less harmful." The decades-old criminalization of personal consumption has failed to stop the plant's cultivation and distribution, the group said. The commission urged that all current criminal prosecution be aimed at drug cartels and organized crime and not marijuana smokers, EFE said. Zedillo did not attend the news conference but worked on the report, Cardoso said. Wednesday's recommendation was the second time in less than a week that a Latin American government official called for decriminalization. A mayor in Peru suggested Friday that the federal government legalize illicit drugs and administer them through the national health ministry. Gusto Sierra, the mayor of the Surquillo district in Lima, said a federal drug law is hypocritical because it allows maximum legally allowed quantities for some drugs and plants but doesn't say where to acquire them, the Peru 21 newspaper reported in a front-page story headlined "Say yes to drugs?" Sierra said he will take the matter up with the nation's executive branch. Zedillo served as president of Mexico from 1994-2000. Gaviria was president of Colombia from 1990-94. And Cardoso led Brazil from 1995-2002.

RIO DE JANEIRO, Brazil (CNN) — Former presidents of Mexico, Colombia, and Brazil called Wednesday for the decriminalization of marijuana for personal use and for a shift in strategy in the war on drugs, according to a Spanish news agency.

People marched in support of legalized marijuana in late January in Belem, northern Brazil.

Former Mexican President Ernesto Zedillo, former Colombian President César Gaviria, and former Brazilian President Fernando Henrique Cardoso made the announcement at a meeting in Brazil of the Latin American Commission on Drugs and Democracy, the EFE news agency reported.

“The problem is that current policies are based on prejudices and fears and not on results,” Gaviria said at a news conference where the commission’s recommendations were presented.

The 17-member panel worked on the report for a year and will send it to all Latin American governments, as well as to the United States and the European Union, EFE said.

Gaviria said the time is right to begin a debate on the issue, particularly given the pragmatic openings created by the election of President Barack Obama in the United States.

“In many states in the United States, as is the case in California, they have begun to change federal policies with regard to tolerating marijuana for therapeutic purposes. And in Washington there’s some consensus that the current policy is failing,” EFE quoted Gaviria as saying.

Decriminalization should be accompanied by treatment for addicts and public service campaigns aimed at preventing abuse, the commission said.

“If you don’t help those who are dependent, you are half way there because they are going to commit crime to get money and pay for the drug,” Gaviria said.

Cardoso said the group called only for the decriminalization of marijuana, not other illicit drugs, because “you have to start somewhere” and it would have been unrealistic to seek the same approach for all drugs, EFE reported.

Marijuana was chosen because it is grown in all countries in the region and because it is “less harmful.” The group said decades-old criminalization of personal consumption has failed to halt the plant’s cultivation and distribution.

The commission urged that current criminal prosecutions be directed at drug cartels and organized crime, rather than marijuana users, EFE said.

Zedillo did not attend the news conference but contributed to the report, Cardoso said.

Wednesday’s recommendation marked the second time in less than a week that a Latin American government official had called for decriminalization.

On Friday, a mayor in Peru suggested that the federal government legalize illicit drugs and administer them through the national health ministry.

Gusto Sierra, mayor of the Surquillo district in Lima, said a federal drug law is hypocritical because it allows maximum legal quantities for some drugs and plants but does not specify where they may be obtained, the Peru 21 newspaper reported in a front-page story headlined “Say yes to drugs?”

Sierra said he would raise the matter with the nation’s executive branch.

Zedillo served as president of Mexico from 1994 to 2000. Gaviria was president of Colombia from 1990 to 1994. Cardoso led Brazil from 1995 to 2002.
outputs.L2:
RIO DE JANEIRO, Brazil (CNN) — Three former Latin American presidents urged on Wednesday that marijuana possession for personal consumption be decriminalized and that governments rethink their approach to the fight against drugs, according to the Spanish news agency EFE.

In late January, demonstrators in Belem, in northern Brazil, marched in favor of legalizing marijuana.

The appeal came from former Mexican President Ernesto Zedillo, former Colombian President Cesar Gaviria and former Brazilian President Fernando Henrique Cardoso. EFE reported that they issued the statement during a meeting in Brazil of the Latin American Commission on Drugs and Democracy.

At a news conference where the commission’s proposals were unveiled, Gaviria said existing drug policies are driven by “prejudices and fears” rather than by evidence of success.

EFE said the commission, made up of 17 members, spent a year preparing its report. The document is to be sent to governments throughout Latin America, as well as to the United States and the European Union.

Gaviria said the moment was appropriate to open a discussion on drug policy, especially given what he described as the practical possibilities created by Barack Obama’s election as U.S. president.

EFE quoted Gaviria as saying that several U.S. states, including California, had already begun moving away from federal policy by allowing marijuana use for medical reasons. He also said there was some agreement in Washington that the existing strategy was not working.

The commission said decriminalization should be paired with addiction treatment and public information campaigns aimed at preventing drug abuse.

Gaviria argued that helping people with drug dependence is essential, saying that without support, addicts may turn to crime to obtain money to buy drugs.

Cardoso said the proposal focused only on marijuana, rather than all illegal substances, because “you have to start somewhere.” According to EFE, he added that asking for decriminalization of every drug would not have been realistic.

The commission selected marijuana because it is cultivated in every country in the region and because it is considered “less harmful.” The group said decades of criminal penalties for personal use have not succeeded in ending marijuana cultivation or distribution.

EFE reported that the commission recommended directing criminal prosecution toward drug cartels and organized crime groups, rather than people who smoke marijuana.

Zedillo was not present at the news conference, but Cardoso said he had participated in preparing the report.

Wednesday’s proposal marked the second time in under a week that a Latin American public official had advocated decriminalization.

The previous Friday, a mayor in Peru suggested that the national government legalize illegal drugs and distribute them through the country’s health ministry.

Gusto Sierra, mayor of Lima’s Surquillo district, told the newspaper Peru 21 that federal drug law is contradictory because it sets maximum legal amounts for certain drugs and plants but does not explain where people can obtain them. The newspaper ran the story on its front page under the headline “Say yes to drugs?”

Sierra said he planned to raise the issue with Peru’s executive branch.

Zedillo was president of Mexico from 1994 to 2000. Gaviria governed Colombia from 1990 to 1994. Cardoso was president of Brazil from 1995 to 2002.

Former presidents of Mexico, Colombia, and Brazil have called for the decriminalization of marijuana for personal use, arguing that Latin America needs a new approach to drug policy. They urged governments to rethink the tactics used in the war on drugs, saying that current strategies have failed to reduce drug consumption, trafficking, and violence in the region.

The proposal was put forward by the Latin American Commission on Drugs and Democracy, a group that has examined the impact of drug policies across the region. The commission argued that many existing policies are shaped more by prejudice and fear than by evidence or measurable results. According to the group, governments should move away from purely punitive approaches and adopt policies that are more realistic, effective, and focused on public health.

The commission plans to send its recommendations to governments throughout Latin America, as well as to the United States and the European Union. Its members hope to encourage a broader international debate about drug policy and to promote alternatives to the traditional enforcement-based model.

The former leaders emphasized that decriminalizing marijuana should not mean ignoring the risks of drug use. They said any change in the law should be accompanied by stronger addiction treatment programs and public education campaigns aimed at preventing abuse, especially among young people. In their view, drug use should be treated more as a public health issue than solely as a criminal matter.

The group chose to focus only on marijuana because it is widely grown in Latin America, is generally considered less harmful than other illegal drugs, and represents a more realistic starting point for reform. By beginning with marijuana, the commission believes governments may be able to test a new approach while reducing some of the social and criminal costs associated with current drug laws.

Former presidents of Mexico, Colombia, and Brazil called for a major change in Latin America’s approach to drug policy, arguing that the region’s long-running “war on drugs” has failed to reduce consumption, trafficking, or the violence associated with illegal markets. Speaking through the Latin American Commission on Drugs and Democracy, they urged governments to consider decriminalizing marijuana for personal use and to move away from policies centered primarily on punishment.

The commission argued that drug use should be treated less as a criminal justice issue and more as a public health problem. Instead of relying on arrests and imprisonment for users, governments should focus on prevention, education, treatment, and harm reduction. The former leaders said that current policies have often filled prisons with low-level offenders while doing little to weaken powerful criminal organizations that profit from prohibition.

They emphasized that decriminalizing marijuana would not mean approving or encouraging drug use. Rather, they described it as a pragmatic step that could allow authorities to redirect resources toward combating organized crime and providing better support for people struggling with addiction. By separating personal marijuana use from more serious drug trafficking offenses, governments could reduce the burden on police, courts, and prison systems.

The commission also called for a more open and evidence-based debate on drug policy. It argued that fear, ideology, and political pressure have too often shaped decisions, while scientific research and public health experience have been ignored. According to the former presidents, Latin America needs policies that are realistic, measurable, and focused on reducing harm rather than simply maintaining strict prohibition.

They said marijuana decriminalization could be a first step toward broader reform. While not presented as a complete solution to drug-related violence or addiction, it was described as a practical measure that could help reduce unnecessary criminalization, weaken illegal markets, and improve the effectiveness of government responses. The commission urged regional leaders to confront the shortcomings of existing strategies and to consider alternatives better suited to protecting public safety, public health, and democratic institutions.

counterfactuals.output:
**Former Latin American presidents call for marijuana decriminalization, shift in drug policy**

Former presidents from Latin America are urging governments to rethink decades of anti-drug policy, calling for the decriminalization of marijuana and a broader move away from what they describe as a failed “war on drugs.”

The appeal, led by former Brazilian President Fernando Henrique Cardoso, former Colombian President César Gaviria and former Mexican President Ernesto Zedillo, argues that current strategies centered on prohibition, militarized enforcement and mass arrests have not significantly reduced drug consumption or trafficking. Instead, they say, those policies have fueled violence, strengthened organized crime and overwhelmed criminal justice systems across the region.

In a report by the Latin American Commission on Drugs and Democracy, the former leaders said marijuana should be treated differently from harder drugs and that personal use should be addressed as a public health issue rather than a criminal matter.

“Prohibitionist policies based on repression have not produced the expected results,” the commission said, calling for “a new paradigm” that places more emphasis on prevention, treatment and harm reduction.

The recommendations come as Latin American countries continue to grapple with drug-related violence, particularly in nations that serve as major production or transit routes for cocaine and other illicit substances. Mexico, Colombia and parts of Central America have seen cartels and trafficking organizations expand their influence despite years of aggressive law enforcement campaigns backed in part by the United States.

The former presidents argued that decriminalizing marijuana could free police and courts to focus on more serious crimes, while reducing the profits available to criminal groups. They stopped short of calling for full legalization of all drugs, but urged governments to experiment with alternative policies and to open a regional debate that includes the United States and Europe, where much of the demand for illegal drugs originates.

Supporters of reform say the call is significant because it comes from former heads of state who once oversaw tough anti-drug policies themselves. Their shift reflects growing frustration in Latin America over the human and economic costs of drug enforcement.

Critics, however, warn that decriminalization could increase drug use and send the wrong message to young people. Some officials also argue that easing marijuana laws without broader international coordination could complicate efforts to combat trafficking networks.

The debate has gained momentum in recent years as several countries and U.S. states have relaxed marijuana laws, while public health experts have increasingly questioned the effectiveness of criminal penalties for users.

The former presidents say their goal is not to minimize the dangers of drug abuse, but to push governments toward policies they believe are more realistic and less damaging.

“Drug policy should be based on evidence, not ideology,” the commission said, urging leaders to prioritize reducing violence, protecting public health and weakening criminal organizations.

counterfactuals.output:
**RIO DE JANEIRO —** A high-profile panel of former Latin American presidents called for a dramatic shift in the region’s drug policy on Wednesday, urging governments to decriminalize marijuana possession for personal use and abandon what it described as a failed “war on drugs.”

The **Latin American Commission on Drugs and Democracy**, led by former presidents **Fernando Henrique Cardoso of Brazil**, **César Gaviria of Colombia** and **Ernesto Zedillo of Mexico**, said decades of prohibitionist policies had failed to curb drug consumption while strengthening organized crime, fueling violence and overwhelming justice systems across the hemisphere.

Presenting its recommendations in Rio de Janeiro, the commission said marijuana should be treated differently from harder drugs and that users should not be criminalized. It also called for drug dependence to be addressed as a public-health issue rather than primarily as a law-enforcement problem.

“The war on drugs has failed,” Gaviria said, arguing that governments must be willing to consider alternatives to policies centered on repression. He said criminalizing consumers had not reduced demand and had instead contributed to prison overcrowding and social marginalization. “We must break the taboo,” he added, saying the debate over drug policy in Latin America had too often been constrained by ideology and fear of political backlash.

Gaviria, who governed Colombia from 1990 to 1994 during one of the bloodiest periods of the battle against the Medellín and Cali cartels, said the region’s experience showed that enforcement alone could not defeat the drug trade. “If we continue doing what we have done, we will continue getting the same results,” he said.

The commission’s report, titled **“Drugs and Democracy: Toward a Paradigm Shift,”** recommends that governments consider the **decriminalization of marijuana possession for personal use**, expand prevention and treatment programs, and focus police and judicial resources on violent criminal networks rather than low-level users.

Cardoso, Brazil’s president from 1995 to 2002, said the commission was not advocating a free-for-all or denying the harms caused by drug abuse. Rather, he said, it was urging a more realistic policy based on evidence, public health and democratic accountability. Cardoso argued that marijuana’s illegality had helped sustain illegal markets without preventing widespread consumption.

Zedillo, who served as Mexico’s president from 1994 to 2000, joined the call at a time when Mexico was facing escalating violence linked to drug-trafficking organizations. The commission said the militarization of anti-drug efforts had placed enormous strain on democratic institutions and had often failed to dismantle the economic foundations of the narcotics trade.

The panel emphasized that Latin America has borne a disproportionate share of the costs of global prohibition. Producer and transit countries, it said, have faced corruption, armed violence, human-rights abuses and weakened rule of law, while demand for illegal drugs has persisted in consumer markets in the United States, Europe and elsewhere.

The report stops short of calling for the legalization of all drugs, but it urges governments to open a broad debate on alternatives to prohibition. It says marijuana decriminalization could be a first step toward reducing the power of criminal groups and separating cannabis consumers from markets where more dangerous drugs are sold.

The commission also called for greater investment in education campaigns, harm-reduction programs and treatment services, arguing that drug abuse should be handled similarly to other health risks. It said punitive approaches toward users had discouraged people from seeking help and had deepened social inequalities.

The recommendations are likely to be controversial in a region where drug policy has long been shaped by pressure from Washington and by fears of appearing soft on crime. But the stature of the commission’s leaders gives the proposal unusual political weight. All three former presidents governed countries deeply affected by the drug trade and have firsthand experience with the limits of enforcement-heavy strategies.

Gaviria said the commission hoped to encourage a more honest discussion across the Americas. “The problem is not going to disappear,” he said. “But we can reduce the harm it causes if we stop treating drug users as criminals and start confronting organized crime with smarter policies.”

The commission’s message from Rio was clear: Latin America, after decades on the front lines of the drug war, should lead the search for a new approach.

Former presidents Ernesto Zedillo of Mexico, César Gaviria of Colombia, and Fernando Henrique Cardoso of Brazil have voiced support for decriminalizing marijuana possession for personal use in Latin America, according to a report by EFE.

The three former leaders argue that the region’s longstanding “war on drugs” has failed to curb drug trafficking, violence, and consumption. Instead, they say drug policy should shift away from a primarily punitive approach and toward public health, prevention, education, and treatment.

Their position does not amount to a blanket endorsement of drug legalization. Rather, they support treating marijuana use as a health and social issue instead of a criminal one, particularly when it involves personal consumption. They contend that criminal penalties for users overcrowd prisons, stigmatize individuals, and do little to weaken organized crime.

Zedillo, Gaviria, and Cardoso have been prominent voices in regional debates over drug policy, emphasizing that Latin America has paid a heavy price for prohibitionist strategies through violence, corruption, and the strengthening of criminal networks. They argue that new approaches are needed, including decriminalization measures, stronger institutions, and policies aimed at reducing harm.

The EFE report highlights a growing discussion across Latin America over whether governments should reconsider strict anti-drug laws, especially regarding marijuana. Supporters of reform say decriminalization could allow authorities to focus resources on combating major trafficking organizations rather than prosecuting low-level users. Critics, however, warn that easing penalties could increase consumption or send the wrong public message.

The former presidents’ stance adds political weight to calls for a reassessment of drug policy in the region, where many countries continue to face the social and security consequences of drug trafficking and prohibition-driven enforcement.

counterfactuals.output:
**Latin American leaders press drug policy rethink, urge focus on cartels over users**

**BOGOTA, Colombia (AP)** — Latin American leaders, long on the front lines of the U.S.-backed war on drugs, are intensifying calls for a shift in policy that treats addiction as a public health issue, reduces prison terms for low-level users and concentrates law enforcement resources on the transnational cartels that profit from trafficking.

The debate, once largely confined to academics and former presidents, has moved into the center of regional diplomacy as governments confront record drug seizures, overcrowded prisons, rising overdose risks and the continuing power of criminal networks despite decades of eradication campaigns and interdiction efforts.

At a regional policy forum this week, presidents, ministers and public health officials from across Latin America said the prevailing approach has punished the weakest links in the drug economy while failing to dismantle the organizations that finance corruption, control territory and move cocaine, synthetic opioids and other drugs through global markets.

“We cannot keep measuring success only by hectares eradicated, tons seized or people imprisoned,” one senior Latin American official said. “If our prisons are full of consumers, couriers and poor farmers, and the cartels remain intact, then the strategy is not working.”

The renewed push comes amid a broader reassessment that began gaining diplomatic space during the administration of U.S. President Barack Obama. While Washington did not abandon prohibition, Obama-era officials signaled greater openness to discussions on alternatives, including public health approaches, sentencing reform and state-level marijuana legalization in the United States. That shift, Latin American leaders say, helped loosen a long-standing taboo around questioning the punitive model promoted for decades through U.S. counternarcotics aid.

Several officials said the region is not calling for a single policy, but for flexibility: expanded treatment for people with substance-use disorders, decriminalization or reduced penalties for possession in some cases, alternatives to incarceration for low-level offenders and more aggressive prosecution of money laundering, arms trafficking, political corruption and cartel leadership.

Public health ministers at the meeting argued that addiction services remain dangerously underfunded. In many countries, treatment is available mainly through private clinics, religious organizations or overcrowded public facilities. Rural areas and poor urban neighborhoods often have little access to evidence-based care.

“Drug dependence is not solved with a prison cell,” said a health official from the Andean region. “It requires prevention, mental health care, medication where appropriate, family support and reintegration into work and school.”

Advocates of reform say Latin America has paid a disproportionate price for global drug demand. Mexico has endured years of cartel violence tied to smuggling routes into the United States. Colombia remains the world’s largest producer of cocaine despite billions of dollars spent on eradication and interdiction. Central American nations have seen gangs and trafficking groups exploit weak institutions and migration routes. Caribbean countries continue to struggle with maritime smuggling and money laundering.

At the same time, officials said, criminal organizations have become more sophisticated. Cartels increasingly operate as multinational businesses, using encrypted communications, shell companies, professional money launderers and alliances with local gangs. Some groups have diversified into extortion, illegal mining, human smuggling and fuel theft.

That evolution, reform advocates argue, makes it even more important to distinguish between drug users and organized crime.

“Police and prosecutors should not be spending their limited resources chasing the person with a small quantity for personal use,” said a former justice minister attending the forum. “They should be following the money, seizing assets, dismantling logistics networks and prosecuting those who order killings, corrupt officials and ship tons of drugs.”

The policy shift is not without opposition. Conservative lawmakers, police unions and some community leaders warn that relaxing penalties could increase consumption, weaken deterrence and send the wrong message to young people. They argue that countries already struggling with violence and weak rule of law cannot afford to appear lenient.

“Cartels will exploit any opening,” said one opposition legislator. “Before changing drug laws, governments must prove they can protect communities and stop criminal groups from expanding.”

U.S. officials have also walked a careful line. Under Obama, Washington supported criminal justice reform at home, encouraged drug courts and treatment programs, and acknowledged that demand in the United States fueled violence abroad. But the United States continued to fund interdiction, extraditions, crop eradication and security cooperation with regional allies.

Latin American diplomats say that mixed posture nonetheless marked an important change from earlier decades, when calls to debate legalization or decriminalization were often treated as politically unacceptable. The Obama administration’s response to state marijuana legalization — allowing regulated markets in Colorado and Washington to proceed under federal guidance — was closely watched across the hemisphere.

For leaders in countries that had been urged for years to militarize drug enforcement, the U.S. experiment raised an uncomfortable question: if parts of the United States could regulate cannabis, why were Latin American countries expected to continue bearing the costs of strict prohibition without debate?

Uruguay became the first country in the world to legalize and regulate recreational marijuana in 2013. Colombia, Mexico, Argentina and others have adopted varying degrees of decriminalization, medical cannabis regulation or court-mandated protections for personal use. But implementation has been uneven, and cocaine, methamphetamine and synthetic opioids remain at the center of security concerns.

Experts say the most difficult reforms involve not cannabis but the broader architecture of drug enforcement: how to define personal possession, how to prevent low-level sellers from being treated the same as violent traffickers, how to provide treatment without coercion, and how to build financial investigations strong enough to hurt cartel profits.

A recurring theme at the forum was prison overcrowding. Across the region, drug offenses account for a significant share of incarcerated people, including women arrested as couriers or for small-scale sales. Human rights groups say many are poor, nonviolent and easily replaced by trafficking networks, making their imprisonment costly and ineffective.

“Every time a low-level courier is arrested, another person takes the job,” said a representative of a regional legal aid organization. “But the children of that courier lose a parent, the prison system becomes more crowded and the criminal structure remains in business.”

Some governments are considering expanded use of diversion programs that send people arrested for possession or minor drug-related offenses into treatment, counseling or community service rather than jail. Others are reviewing sentencing laws to distinguish more clearly between users, small-scale sellers, transporters, armed traffickers and cartel organizers.

Public health specialists cautioned, however, that treatment cannot simply become another arm of punishment. They said compulsory treatment programs have often produced poor outcomes and, in some cases, abuses. Effective policy, they said, requires voluntary care, harm reduction, overdose prevention and long-term social support.

The rise of synthetic drugs has added urgency. While Latin America’s traditional role has been as a producer and transit region for cocaine and cannabis, officials are increasingly concerned about fentanyl, methamphetamine and chemical precursors. Mexico has faced intense U.S. pressure over fentanyl trafficking, while South American governments are monitoring the spread of synthetic substances in urban nightlife and local markets.

That changing drug landscape has strengthened calls for intelligence-led policing rather than broad crackdowns. Security officials said priority should be placed on high-value investigations: cartel command structures, cross-border arms flows, precursor chemical suppliers, corrupt port operators, clandestine airstrips, maritime routes and illicit finance.

Several leaders also called on consumer countries, especially the United States and Europe, to do more to reduce demand and stop the southbound flow of firearms and dirty money. They argued that Latin American governments are often judged by drug supply indicators while wealthy nations face less scrutiny for consumption, weapons trafficking and financial systems used to launder profits.

“The responsibility is shared, but the burden has not been shared equally,” one Caribbean diplomat said. “Our police intercept boats, our courts process cases, our communities face violence. But the profits are banked elsewhere, and the guns come from elsewhere.”

Analysts say a regional consensus is still far off. Latin American countries vary widely in politics, institutions, violence levels and public attitudes toward drugs. A government facing open conflict with cartels may have little appetite for decriminalization, while another with lower violence may focus on health and regulation.

Even so, the tone of the debate has changed. Few leaders now defend the old model without qualification. Many still support aggressive action against trafficking organizations, but they increasingly pair that stance with calls for treatment, prevention, sentencing reform and alternatives to incarceration.

The result is an emerging middle ground: not a wholesale legalization of all drugs, but a recalibration of priorities.

“We are not talking about surrendering to organized crime,” said one senior justice official. “We are talking about being smarter. The user needs help. The addict needs treatment. The farmer needs alternatives. The cartel boss needs prosecution. And the state needs to know the difference.”

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a CNN news piece with dateline RIO DE JANEIRO about ex-presidents of Mexico, Colombia, and Brazil urging marijuana decriminalization, plus context on a Peruvian mayor’s similar proposal.
counterfactuals.output:
RIO DE JANEIRO (CNN) — Three former Latin American presidents are urging governments to rethink the region’s drug strategy, calling for the decriminalization of marijuana use as part of a broader effort to reduce violence and weaken organized crime.

Former Mexican President Ernesto Zedillo, former Colombian President César Gaviria and former Brazilian President Fernando Henrique Cardoso said the long-running “war on drugs” has failed to curb consumption or dismantle trafficking networks. The three, who have all led countries deeply affected by drug-related crime, argue that treating drug use primarily as a criminal matter has overcrowded prisons, strained police forces and done little to reduce demand.

Their proposal, released through the Latin American Commission on Drugs and Democracy, does not call for legalizing the drug trade. Instead, it recommends decriminalizing marijuana possession for personal use, expanding treatment for addicts and focusing law enforcement resources on violent criminal organizations.

“The policy of prohibition has produced disastrous results,” the commission said, urging governments to break what it called a taboo around drug-policy debate.

The statement comes as parts of Latin America are increasingly questioning U.S.-backed anti-drug policies that have emphasized eradication, interdiction and criminal prosecution. Mexico has faced a surge in cartel violence, Colombia has spent decades battling drug-funded armed groups, and Brazil continues to confront powerful trafficking gangs in urban areas.

The former presidents said marijuana should be handled differently from harder drugs such as cocaine and heroin, arguing that decriminalization could help separate casual users from criminal markets and allow authorities to concentrate on major traffickers.

Their position echoes a recent proposal from Peru, where a local mayor in Lima’s Miraflores district suggested a similar approach to marijuana. Mayor Manuel Masías argued that decriminalizing or regulating marijuana use could reduce the profits of traffickers and free police to pursue more serious crimes. His comments sparked controversy in Peru, where national officials have traditionally taken a tough stance on narcotics.

Supporters of decriminalization say the debate reflects growing frustration with decades of enforcement-heavy policies. Critics warn that loosening drug laws could increase consumption and send the wrong message to young people.

The commission’s recommendations are not binding, but the involvement of three former heads of state gives the proposal unusual political weight in a region where drug trafficking has shaped domestic security, foreign policy and relations with the United States for generations.
